utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber was informed that the Defence wanted to raise a preliminary issue. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to our colleagues from the Prosecution. This Defence has to point out for the record the problem we are facing in today's intention to examine the witness who was planned for the first part of our session. Just to remind you, Your Honours, in our submission from July 2013, after your decision regarding our submission from April 2013, we pointed out that this Defence believes today's testimony would not be according to the rules. Let me remind you of two rules that were quoted in the submission. First of all, this witness has to did testify about the communication that happened during the court recess between the client and his defendants; i.e., the communication which is privileged, which is protected and which cannot be used in any proceedings whatsoever. The second reason and we remind you that we mentioned it in our submission, is the fact that today's witness is a prosecutor's office's staff member and, as such, at that moment she was in the courtroom and she was listening to the communication between the client and his counsel beyond and outside of the official part of the trial. Bearing all this in mind, we believe that she would be in direct conflict of interest because she is a staff member, she is sitting on the side opposite to us in this courtroom and now she has been called to testify in order to prove the mens rea that our client possibly had. These two arguments is something that we emphasised in July 2013 in our submission, and the reply is still pending from you, and still, the hearing of this witness has been planned for today. We would kindly ask you to render a decision on that first before the witness may be called into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Very briefly in response, the position of the Prosecution is that Mr. Mladic waived his right to that privilege by yelling the words across the courtroom. This was something that was put on the record on the 23rd of August, 2012, at page 1482 where Mr. Mladic was warned that if he were to yell something across the courtroom, he may be subject to that as evidence against him. Furthermore on the issue of Ms. Karall being an OTP staff member, that, we submit, goes to issues of credibility and not to admissibility. Just like with other OTP witnesses the Defence is free to challenge Ms. Karall in cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, any reply to what the Prosecution just submitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. I know what your position was with regard to everything that General Mladic has to say. I would like to remind you that we were told that any communication during trial may be on post-it notes and what happens during the breaks is not part of your decision. On several occasions, you suggested that the communication between us and our client should take part during the break, not during the trial. If it has to be during the trial, it has to be on post-it notes. It has to be at very low tone, and this communication happened between the client and the counsel once he left the courtroom during the break and the witness who has been called to testify today heard that communication, which was during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just re-reading what happened on 23 August of last year. Do you have a specific line reference, Ms. Marcus? I saw that there was a --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I was referring to page 1481.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And where --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The transcript says 1482, perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: It's line 19 where Judge Moloto commented on the waiver of the privilege.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then one question, Mr. Stojanovic. What is the legal authority that if you shout audible for everyone but not in the presence of the Bench, that that then suddenly that other rules would apply? And that you would not have given up your privilege if you shout in the -- or yell in the presence of other persons than the Bench? Is there any legal authority for that? Or could you analyse the waiver of the privilege in such a way that it does only apply during court sessions and not if you do it anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the basis for this position on the part of the Defence is this: First of all, it is our national legislation and the rules of the state from which the counsel come. The law on legal representation and the code of conduct of lawyers regulates the issue of relationship between a client and his counsel. Everything that a client communicates to his counsel is privileged. According to the code of conduct of Defence counsel, the counsel is duty-bound to keep it to himself and cannot use it for any other purposes save for his contacts with his client. Second of all, it doesn't say anywhere that the mere fact that that communication is aloud is proof that there is a waiver on the privilege that exists. Communication is a communication. Every day we are in a position to communicate with our client and I don't think that it is at all in dispute that he has to speak aloud because of his health problems, because of his condition. This is as regards our relationship with our client. We are accustomed to it. Second of all, you know, Your Honours, that our communication in the Detention Unit is also considered privileged. It is recorded but it is not used for any purpose or in any stage of the proceedings in any case. And that applies across the board. Irrespective of the fact whether the communication is loud, at a high volume, on the border of verging of misunderstandings on our part, but this is part of our job and we have to do it every day, literally, Your Honours. That is why I believe that this was communication between the client and his Defence counsel, and that in that sense it was never meant to suggest that our client waived his right to privileged communication with his counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those further submissions. Same question for that OTP staff, if they hear anything, that they are not qualified any further to testify about it. Is there any basis for that submission? Any legal basis? I'm not seeking an explanation but whether you have any legal authority for that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. This could be the basis that concerned the status of the lady who is supposed to testify today. We claim that she is in direct conflict of interest, and this may be an argument for the cross-examination and for the credibility of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Both the objections are denied. The first objection about the waiver of the privileged communication, the argument ignores that by speaking very loudly, that the communication cannot be considered to be confidential any further, and the accused has been warned about that, or at least it has been brought to his attention. For the second issue, there is no conflict of interest. The witness who will appear is supposed to testify about facts, nothing more, nothing less, and I take it, Ms. Marcus, that you'll keep that in mind. The witness is not here to establish any mens rea or things of the kind. The witness is just here to tell the Court upon being examined what she saw, heard or experienced otherwise. She is a witness of fact. Therefore, the -- both the objections to hear this witness are denied. And the usher is requested to escort the witness into the courtroom. As far as protective measures are concerned, there are no protective measures requested for this witness. Nevertheless it may be necessary to go into private session if the content of the testimony is at risk to be prejudicial to other witnesses who testified in -- with protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I've planned it as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Karall.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I can't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I restart. Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not through the ear-phones. I can hear you without them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But if others start speaking in a different language --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll restart. Ms. Karall, before you give evidence, the rules require that you make a solemn declaration, of which the text is now handed out to you. May I invite to you make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Karall, you'll first be examined by Ms. Marcus. Ms. Marcus, as you most likely know already, is counsel for the Prosecution. Ms. Marcus you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Karall.

utterances.speaker: MARIA KARALL
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: MARIA KARALL
utterances.text: My name is Maria Karall.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And what is your date of birth, please?

utterances.speaker: MARIA KARALL
utterances.text: The 5th of March, 1964.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: MARIA KARALL
utterances.text: I was born in Austria, my birth place is called Oberpullendorf.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could you spell the location of your birth just for the transcript, please?

utterances.speaker: MARIA KARALL
utterances.text: O-b-e-r-p-u-l-l-e-n-d-o-r-f.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly speak closer to the microphone, please? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you adjust the microphone a little bit further down, that might help. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Ms. Karall, what language do you consider to be your mother tongue?

utterances.speaker: MARIA KARALL
utterances.text: It's Croatian. The area where I come from has a national minority, there are several Croatian villages, so I grew up in a Croatian village.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Chamber a bit about the kind of Croatian which is your mother tongue?

utterances.speaker: MARIA KARALL
utterances.text: Well, the local dialect that we speak is a bit outdated. The minority that moved there 500 years ago still uses the language that was used there 500 years ago so it is Croatian but it's archaic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Did you ever have occasion to formally study B/C/S as well?

utterances.speaker: MARIA KARALL
utterances.text: Yes. I had an education in school, in high school, for six years.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: What other languages do you speak fluently?

utterances.speaker: MARIA KARALL
utterances.text: I'm fluent in English. Of course my best language is German because it's the language I was educated in. I'm fluent in English and in Dutch. I have a certain knowledge of French and Russian.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Ms. Karall, how long have you worked at the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MARIA KARALL
utterances.text: I've been here for more than 15 years, since the 1st of May, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And in what capacity?

utterances.speaker: MARIA KARALL
utterances.text: My job title is language reference assistant.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can you describe for us what that entails?

utterances.speaker: MARIA KARALL
utterances.text: It's a whole range of duties. I mainly started interpreting for the investigators. I also do written translations, transcripts, lately I've been more into administration, and the last years I've been the witness co-ordinator for the Mladic team which includes contacting witnesses, organising that they come here on time, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: In the course of your duties, have you been requested to transcribe B/C/S, which is spoken on audio or video?

utterances.speaker: MARIA KARALL
utterances.text: Yes. I've been transcribing interviews that the OTP did. I've been transcribing videos, intercepts, in B/C/S and in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Ms. Karall, as you know, you've been called as a witness before this Chamber because of the events which took place in this trial's hearing of 18th of February, 2013. On that day, what was requested of you by the Prosecution team?

utterances.speaker: MARIA KARALL
utterances.text: I was asked to be in court to monitor the accused in case he says something that might offend the witness on the stand.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: During what period of that day were you present in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: MARIA KARALL
utterances.text: I was present from the beginning of the first session to the middle of the break after the first session.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Did you, in fact, note down some words which you heard uttered by the accused on that day?

utterances.speaker: MARIA KARALL
utterances.text: Yes, I did. As soon as I heard them, I jotted down a few notes in English in my notebook, and later on I put a formal note in an e-mail to my team to inform the team, in B/C/S and with my translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: How was it that you were able to hear the words spoken by the accused?

utterances.speaker: MARIA KARALL
utterances.text: Well, I was sitting where now -- it was in the same courtroom. I would have been sitting behind Mr. McCloskey, although he wasn't present that day, and the accused is just across of me, and I can hear him very well because he speaks loudly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just to -- for the record, Mr. McCloskey is sitting one row before the interpreters' booth which is close to the door where the Judges enter the courtroom, and what the witness explains is that she was seated at the row closest to those booths. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could the Court Officer please call up 65 ter 30274 but not broadcast it to the public. This is the e-mail which was sent by Ms. Karall which she just referred to. I've discussed this with Mr. Stojanovic before the hearing, and he has said that he has no objection to it being added to the exhibit list and used and tendered.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Ms. Karall, without reading any of the contents yet is this the e-mail that you sent to the Prosecution team after hearing the words of the accused on the 18th of February, 2013?

utterances.speaker: MARIA KARALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could we have private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Ms. Marcus, we know where the witness was seated at the time, where the accused is is common knowledge between -- among everyone who sits in this courtroom. Would there be any -- would it be good to establish approximately the distance or whether the parties would agree on the distance between the witness listening and the accused speaking?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Would you like me to ask the witness to estimate the distance or would Your Honour like to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: An estimate of the witness is fine. I'd rather that you agree. You can measure it before you agree so that there is no -- we don't have to rely on a great talent or a bad talent in estimating distances.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I'm sure we can measure it and agree from our position, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we would like to hear from you after the next break.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Ms. Karall, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions for the witness, but I would like to make a bar table submission following the end of her testimony with leave of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll hear from you after the examination of the witness. Mr. Stojanovic, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Karall, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Stojanovic, as most likely is known to you as well, is counsel for Mr. Mladic. You may proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Ms. Karall. Just a few questions that I want to put to you. Before that day, the 18th of February, 2013, had you ever been in this courtroom during the Mladic trial?

utterances.speaker: MARIA KARALL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who tasked you to be in the courtroom on that day and follow or monitor the accused?

utterances.speaker: MARIA KARALL
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At any moment during your many years of service at the Tribunal, had you ever been given such a specific task from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MARIA KARALL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During the first hour of the session, did you notice Mr. Mladic addressing any words to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MARIA KARALL
utterances.text: No, not during the court session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What was the specific task you received from Ms. Marcus?

utterances.speaker: MARIA KARALL
utterances.text: I was to listen to whatever the accused might say that might offend the witness or also observe whether he does any gestures or anything like that, and also listen to whatever he says during the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You did not notice any gestures during the first session on Mr. Mladic's part directed at the witness, did you?

utterances.speaker: MARIA KARALL
utterances.text: No, not during the court session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Observing him, did you notice on his face a redness of the skin, any sign of anxiety, anything that would indicate his involvement in the trial?

utterances.speaker: MARIA KARALL
utterances.text: No, I can't remember that. I mean, he would not have liked whatever he said, but and he wouldn't have been smiling or anything like that or be relaxed, but, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The words that you mentioned a moment ago, did Mr. Mladic utter them after all the three members of the Chamber had left the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: MARIA KARALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Those words, were they uttered by Mr. Mladic after the witness was ushered out of the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: MARIA KARALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did he say that while sitting down, while he was standing up, or at the moment when he was being taken out?

utterances.speaker: MARIA KARALL
utterances.text: I think he already stood up, he had called you to the Bench to talk to his lawyers, I don't know whether you were present or Mr. Lukic or it would have been Mr. Ivetic, I think, and he was talking to his lawyers, and I think that you were all on your feet already and then went out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Those words, were they addressed to his Defence counsel whom he had invited to approach a moment before?

utterances.speaker: MARIA KARALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you tell us if you remember who at that moment, apart from the counsel, the security, you and General Mladic, was in the courtroom, if anyone?

utterances.speaker: MARIA KARALL
utterances.text: Mr. Groome was here. He was still sitting and making notes. I think Ms. Marcus had left the room already. There might have been an intern left, perhaps the court reporter. I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were all the three Defence counsel present today present at that time, or was any of us missing then?

utterances.speaker: MARIA KARALL
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, I should like us to see an excerpt, because there is a recording made available to us by the OTP, and the recording resulted from your prior order for General Mladic to be recorded, and I would like to play that part of the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do, could I ask one additional question? When you told us who was still in court, you didn't mention representative of the Registry, Chambers, assistant from Chambers. Do you have any recollection on whether those were still present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember but I think that everybody had already left. The security might have -- security guards might have -- would have been in the court but I think nobody from the Bench was still here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then, let's look at the recording.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, I should like to ask only for one excerpt, 1:05:10 to 1:07:05. There is no audio, just the video footage, and then I will put my questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Maria, after seeing this excerpt, precisely the moments that you testify about, do you stand by your testimony to the effect that the words you just quoted were uttered by Mr. Mladic while standing up or sitting down, addressing the three of us?

utterances.speaker: MARIA KARALL
utterances.text: I really can't say. I don't know whether he was partly -- whether he was sitting when he started to speak and then stood up. I can't say when exactly he said the words.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the words that you cited, it is said Mr. Mladic mentioned a photograph. You don't know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, if we come to the content of what was heard, out of an abundance of caution I would rather deal with that in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour. I did not mean to go much further, but out of caution, perhaps we should move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps only for very short but we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Karall, after the break, did you return to the courtroom to attend the second session?

utterances.speaker: MARIA KARALL
utterances.text: No. I went up to my office to make a note about what I had heard and to continue with my regular work.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honours, may I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may consult, briefly and at a low volume, your client.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you report these words to Mr. Groome immediately after hearing them, in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: MARIA KARALL
utterances.text: Yes. We went out and we talked about it right in front of the courtroom. I told him, and that's why it went into the record with a slightly different translation than is in my e-mail.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That is what I want to ask you about, and that will be my final question. Did you put down the words you heard the same moment or did you have the opportunity to replay the recording perhaps and record what Mr. Mladic may have said?

utterances.speaker: MARIA KARALL
utterances.text: No. I had to do it from memory. I only heard it once.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, as far as the Chamber is aware, there is no audio recording of the event at all, is there?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know any more, Your Honours. I cannot be sure. We received only a video recording, without the audio, but I would not be surprised that sound is recorded as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is not from this camera which was installed upon the order of the Chamber. Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we reviewed the audio from the floor, which did not capture anything that was said during the breaks so there is no -- as far as I'm concerned, from our perspective, there is no audio recording.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Then I can skip the remaining questions because this was very important.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you whether, in the e-mail message you sent that day and the report that is marked 65 ter 30270, there is a slight semantic difference between what is written in your original e-mail sent out that day and the report that was made available to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if Mr. Stojanovic is asking the witness to compare, he should show her what he's asking her to compare, in our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stojanovic asked whether there is a slight semantic difference, which I think for a reader should be clear so I do not see -- of course, it could be shown to the witness. If there are any follow-up questions, then please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, he is asking the witness -- he quoted 65 ter 30270 which is an information report which was put together after Ms. Karall and Ms. Sokola were interview by an OTP investigator. So he's -- I believe he's asking Ms. Karall to compare what is contained in the information report with what was contained in her e-mail, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you want -- I mean, if the two documents are there, everyone who can read can see any difference so, therefore, that's a relatively useless question. If, however, you want to further explore that difference, then of course you should show it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I hope that Madam Prosecutor and I will agree there is a certain difference, and I thought I would cover it only through a question as to how that difference occurred because it's not in dispute that there is a difference, but now we are receiving an answer from the Prosecution as to how it occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So you say you've answered the question, you accept the explanation of how this -- what the origin of the difference is on the basis of what Ms. Marcus just said. You agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any further questions, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours I have concluded. Thank you very much, Ms. Karall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Fluegge has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Karall, we all watched the video without any audio. First, we could see that Mr. Mladic was sitting, then he stood up, and then slowly left the courtroom. If he had taken that -- that there are three sequences, what we saw in the video, at which time or I should say at which sequence did he utter the words you have heard?

utterances.speaker: MARIA KARALL
utterances.text: It's half a year ago, I don't remember these details. I saw the video for the first time right now. It's obvious that he addressed Mr. Stojanovic because then Mr. Stojanovic -- while sitting, and then Mr. Stojanovic -- because Mr. Stojanovic turned around and went to the Bench. And I think at some point after he stood up, he would have continued with the few sentences. There might have been a few seconds' break between whatever he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Was it while he was standing and addressing his counsel, or was it during the time when he was at the exit door?

utterances.speaker: MARIA KARALL
utterances.text: It must have been that he started speaking while he was sitting, he continued while he was standing up, but after he turned to the exit door and faced the exit door, I wouldn't have heard him anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one additional question about you talked about the archaic language you used in your village, and then you said during second education you were taught normal Croatian. Is that -- you said you learned it later. Is that in school they didn't use that archaic dialect or --

utterances.speaker: MARIA KARALL
utterances.text: Oh, yes, of course we started with the Burgenland Croatian. It's an official language in Austria. You can compare it to Afrikaans and Dutch, if you want to. So Afrikaans being an earlier form or a -- yeah, of Dutch. And then, of course, I had training in school, but then I also had training on the job before I started with the Tribunal, and when I started with the Tribunal I had to pass a language test.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Also, in the Croatian language?

utterances.speaker: MARIA KARALL
utterances.text: At the Tribunal, it was called B/C/S already, so it's not just Croatian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see the point but in modern language and not the archaic language?

utterances.speaker: MARIA KARALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Have you had ever any difficulty in understanding the nowadays Croatian language?

utterances.speaker: MARIA KARALL
utterances.text: Not since I've been with the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you -- you had or?

utterances.speaker: MARIA KARALL
utterances.text: Yes, while I -- before I started school and before I started formal training in the official Croatian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the formal training you got in school again?

utterances.speaker: MARIA KARALL
utterances.text: In high school, what we call gymnasium and I think -- I'm not even sure whether I started with 10 years or with 12 years, whether it was eight years or six years that we had it in school. But in elementary school, when I started reading, we had our first reading books in Croatian and in German, in parallel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that Croatian, was that written modern Croatian?

utterances.speaker: MARIA KARALL
utterances.text: Gradually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Gradually. So it's moved from dialect, from archaic to nowadays Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MARIA KARALL
utterances.text: Yes, and the differences aren't that big.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Have the questions in the cross-examination or questions by the Bench triggered any need for further questions, Ms. Marcus?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then this concludes -- Mr. Stojanovic, have the questions by the Bench triggered any need for further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Ms. Marcus, you announced that you would seek to tender more exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a bar table submission which I can do after the witness is excused, with your leave. I don't think it would be contentious. We discussed it before the session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If that's the case, then we could already release the witness. Ms. Karall, thank you very much for coming. I often have to add "a long way to The Hague," but that might not apply to you. But nevertheless, thank you very much for having come to this courtroom and having answered the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench. You are excused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Prosecution seeks leave to tender into evidence portions of this synchronised video that Mr. Stojanovic played. What we've done is we took -- it's a synchronisation between the floor video of that hearing and the isolated video that was focused on Mr. Mladic. That is why you saw the isolated video on the left side of your screen and a blank on the right because that was not when the Chamber was in session. So what we've done is we have synchronised them and selected very few short clips from that video. We sent the selection to the Defence on -- the latest selection on Monday, the 9th, and Mr. Stojanovic and I discussed this before the hearing began today. And if Mr. Stojanovic has no objections, as I understood, we would seek leave to tender into evidence our selected clips. If the Chamber wishes to see it, we can, if not, I'm happy to just have it tendered into evidence. We have tentatively assigned 65 ter number 30273.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objection against it being admitted, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Considering that our clip is part of that video footage, then it would be pointless for us to tender just the clip we used in the sequence we mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And we looked at your selection from that clip that was when Mr. Mladic first was seated, then stood up, and then left the courtroom. Is that the only portion, Ms. Marcus, where we do not have two simultaneous pictures?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. The selection that we made, which is a total of about four and a half minutes, contains an introductory clip, just so that we can mark the date on which it happened. It contains two very short clips from the hearing of that day, with subtitles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And there we would have the --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: There you would have both, yes. So it needs to be admitted under seal, yes. And then the last clips, clips 4 through 6, show -- okay. Clips 4 and 5 are the beginning of the break and the end of the break. The end of the break being relevant to the evidence of Ms. Sokola, the other quote that was heard from Mr. Mladic. And the final clip, clip 6, is a very short piece from the beginning of the second session, just before Mr. Mladic was removed from the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, what was played is then the beginning of the break?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, that was from clip 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Clip 4 starting at I think it was 1 hour, 5 minutes, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just a few seconds before that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just a few seconds before we see on the picture 1:05, 1 hour, 5 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, I included the exiting of the Chamber so we would be able to set the approximate time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, although --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you're exiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that is not what we looked at but that is part of number 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, this all having been now sufficiently identified, Madam Registrar, to be admitted under seal under what number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30273 receives number P2181, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted under seal. If there is nothing else at this moment, we'll continue after the break with the cross-examination of Mr. Butler. We take a break and we'll resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There was a preliminary matter to be raised by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. With your leave, we understand that before hearing the witness earlier today, you had made a decision pursuant to our submission from July 2013, and you rejected our remarks. We would like certification and the right to interlocutory decision because we are of the opinion that this was privileged communication between the client and his Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, if you want a certificate, file a motion asking for a certificate. That's what you have to do. You don't have to announce that. That's all understood. You're entitled to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. That's correct. Thank you. I didn't know whether to address you in writing because we didn't receive your decision in writing. So we would like to file a written request for certificate on your decision. If that's the case, we are going to send a written motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Next question, have the parties agreed on the distance between the back row there and the accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. There was a joint measuring working group with Mr. Blaskic and a tape measure and we came up with 15.5 metres and for Mr. Ivetic and myself the archaic 50.8 feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the parties agree that that was the distance between the accused and between the witness, Ms. Karall, at the time. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I have a last matter. In relation to Mr. Butler, Madam Registrar meanwhile has provisionally assigned exhibit numbers to documents he had consulted in preparing his report. Have the parties received the list with the 65 ter numbers? The provisionally assigned numbers are, Mr. Ivetic, P2148 up to and including P2160. Is there any objection against those to be admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Insofar as they have now been identified, no. As you might recall, my objection was based upon referring to them as being in the binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, they have been identified. No objections. Madam Registrar, none of them there is any need to have them under seal, I think. Therefore, P2148 up to and including P2160, are admitted into evidence. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, and lastly we do, as you asked, now have a surrogate sheet for the stabiliser fin photo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, that will then be part of this Exhibit P2053. You may add that to the -- to e-court. If there is nothing else, then could Mr. Butler be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, while we are waiting for Mr. Butler to arrive, I just had a conversation with Mr. Lukic, and I realise that I didn't understand whether we are to expect a written decision, or is it today that is the first day before our deadline to submit a motion for interlocutory decision?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will let you know later today or not certainly not later than tomorrow after having reviewed all the details of the submissions that were made.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony and Mr. Ivetic will now continue his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, sir.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Before we take up at the topic where we left off yesterday, I would like to revisit another topic. I'd like to return to the meeting that you testified about yesterday that you had with General Milovanovic, and this would be the one that you either attended with Jean-Rene Ruez or Barry Hogan, which we have established you do not recall being recorded. Can you help us at all about the month or the year that such a meeting would have taken place?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I just -- I just can't remember, recall at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Can you recall at all where, what locale, this meeting was held at; i.e. was it a military building, a hotel, a restaurant, private home? Are you able to provide any details in relation to where the meeting would have been held?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it was in a conference room in a hotel in Banja Luka, if I recall correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could it have been at the Krajina military hotel in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could tell you it wasn't the Krajina Corps headquarters. It could have been the military hotel, but clearly you seem to know more about it than I do, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, sir: Do you recall how many times in total, how many meetings in total, you would have had with General Milovanovic? Was it just that one or were there other --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was just the one, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And are you sure that this meeting had been requested by General Milovanovic rather than being requested by the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding, as it was told to me, was that it was a request of General Milovanovic. Again, I received my information from the chief of Prosecutions on this. I'm sorry, the chief of investigations, Mr. Ralston. You know, I had no foreknowledge of any of these issues. I was simply called into his office one day and said, You're going to Banja Luka in several days and here is why.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough, sir. I'd like to call up 65 ter number 19462. And to see if that can assist you with remembering details. There we go. Sir, these are notes or a record of a meeting, and it's dated -- well, the typed version is dated the 26th of March, but then that's crossed off and it says 27 March 2001, and I can tell you these are notes that are -- that purport to be from General Milovanovic, and I'd like to go through with you the introduction to see if you have knowledge of this meeting. As you can see it says there: "On 26," crossed off-hand, written "27 March 2001, General Milovanovic and his associates held a meeting with representatives of The Hague Tribunal at the request of the guests. The meeting was attended by Mr. Barry Hogan, Mr. Richard Butler, Mr. Ken Corlett, and a translator on behalf of the Tribunal. And alongside General Milovanovic, Colonel Mikajlo Mitrovic, Lieutenant-Colonel Darko Matijasovic, Mr. Zoran Cvetkovic, and Ms. Branka Tanasic as a translator. The meeting was held on the premises of the Krajina military hotel in Banja Luka and commenced at 1000 hours." First of all, sir, does this appear to be the meeting in question or is it another meeting other than the one we were discussing earlier?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. This is the meeting in question, and I now recall that Ken Corlett, who was the ICTY liaison to the RS, was present as well, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And if you would look with me at the fifth paragraph from the top in the English and in the B/C/S, it is recorded here as follows: "Mr. Hogan thanked for the opportunity to attend and began by saying that he first wanted to clarify the circumstances under which this meeting was taking place. As far as he had understood, Ms. Carla Del Ponte, she and Mr. Milovanovic had a conversation in December," crossed out, handwritten, "October, and they talked about the possibility of Mr. Milovanovic giving an interview. When she returned to The Hague and reported on this, Mr. Butler and he were assigned by the Tribunal to contact Mr. Milovanovic. "General Milovanovic went on to say that he considered the conversation informal, and that he had so far had similar conversations on the subject with Mr. Harland, Mr. Graf, and Ms. Del Ponte." Do you recall what Mr. Hogan is recorded as saying, does that refresh your recollection as to matters or is it news to you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, I never knew the circumstances behind what predicated the meeting. I was never given a back story. I was just told to participate, as such, and I can only again testify to what I was told were the circumstances as to why I was selected to go on this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can turn to page 6 of the English, and I believe it's also -- should also be page 6 of the B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, before we look at it any further, could you give any information about the author of this, what seems to be a record of a meeting? Because it's not signed, not dated, not -- there is no name under it. Could you have any -- would you be able to give any information as where it comes from?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I can, Your Honour. I thought I had started off by saying they purport to be the notes of Mr. Milovanovic. That is what is represented to me by the Office of the Prosecutor whose document this is, and it was sent to me by the Office of the Prosecutor after the session. And that's what it says in e-court, so beyond that I obviously can't confirm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I'm not saying that you should, but I'm just wondering where it comes from and what it exactly is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, this has, my understanding, been disclosed long ago, but with the topic and with the many documents I just helped out yesterday and sent it on to the Defence. I don't have independent recollection of it but I also had shown the Defence an interview with General Milovanovic where they begin the interview with a reference to this meeting and the fact that he is turning over a -- Milovanovic turned over this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I'm -- at this moment my simple question was where -- oh, you would say -- you were about to say where it came from. I apologise for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry for being a bit Bosnian in my response, but I meant to be -- at this interview Milovanovic provides his -- his notes of that meeting, and that's all we have of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I certainly would not have interrupted you if you would have said, It was given to us during an interview by Mr. Milovanovic. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't recollect it, I'm just stating what's in the recording of the meeting, and of course we have General Milovanovic coming next so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ivetic, please proceed, and again apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This is the second paragraph in the B/C/S, the first paragraph on the English, sir. And please bear with me as I read it into the record, and then I'll have some questions about it: "General Milovanovic added that for the first testimonies of Serbian officers he requested written guarantees from Ms. Del Ponte, that these officers would not be arrested during or 48 hours after their testimony which was provided and that paved the way for the officers to testify. After that, the response was better and better because the men realised that they were not being summoned to testify just because they were Serbs. In 1999, as Minister of Defence of the RS, he was supposed to pay an official visit to NATO and he asked NATO for a guarantee that during his stay he would not be taken into custody by the Tribunal but he received no guarantee. Mr. Butler added that he often conducted investigations and interviews with people from NATO and that they turned out not to be good collaborators or the greatest of friends. He firmly believes that this letter did not even reach The Hague Tribunal. As for the Tribunal, much attention is given to the protection of witnesses. Copies of the records of conversations are provided and no one should be afraid of giving these testimonies. Instead they should be used to help the Court." Does this writing correspond to any memories you have of the meeting with General Milovanovic that you had discussed with us yesterday?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. One of the issues that was discussed -- and again, looking at the two paragraphs in context, I do recall that when we started the process where the Republika Srpska government would make their officers available to members of the Office of the Prosecutor for interview, that they wanted guarantees that those individuals would not be immediately apprehended. Obviously, you know, in hindsight, if one recalls the case of General Talic, who was attending a military meeting out of the country and was subsequently arrested, I believe, by the Austrians, not an unreasonable request by -- as I think it was in 1999 he was the minister of defence. So one of the things that obviously I did discuss was the fact that, you know, we had obviously a process where the rules of the Tribunal, you know, put certain limits on witness statements and testimonies, and individuals had to be warned, and I believe at the time - I don't know if it is still the case - that in the case of an individual who is suspect, that the transcripts or at least a recording of the interview was provided to the individual in question. So that was from the notes that he's given. It does talk about for the most part the general areas that was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, at the time of this meeting, in March of 2001, General Milovanovic is no longer an official within the government. He's a private citizen; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall exactly what his status was in 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know or recall why this meeting attended by four Tribunal OTP staff and three VRS army officers and two other VRS personnel -- pardon me, RS personnel, would not have been recorded or documented, apart from the notes that are said to come from General Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, my understanding of it was that the primary purpose of the meeting was to deal with procedural issues, not to formally interview the general. Again, I can't tell you why I even was selected to go on this other than presumably he was aware of me from my testimony related to General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now I would like to go back to the topic that we had left off with yesterday in court. As you might recall we had started talking about Kravica, and to make sure that we are all on the same page as to what we are talking about, I'd like to let you know that during the course of this trial, this Chamber has heard evidence of a Prosecution witness, RM374, who gave testimony at transcript page 12775 through 12779, that he heard from a direct eye witness to the event at Kravica, where the detainees being transported on a bus took over control of the weapons of the guards after overpowering them on the bus, and that shooting ensued between both sides, the Serb policemen guards on the one hand and the armed detainees on the other hand that were on the bus, and that he was not sure it was Kravica, although in one of his interviews he had said it was Kravica. Did your review of the evidence and research include this type of occurrence, and is this what you understood when we broached the topic late in the day yesterday?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, to the degree of my research on Kravica, I don't know whether it is in my narrative, I hope it is in my revised narrative because we did -- if we got the information that soon. But certainly I have testified that there are medical records from the Bratunac medical centre reflecting the fact that on 13 July 1995, two individuals -- one individual was wounded who was a member of the Bratunac Red Beret, so I know that's in my narrative, and one RS police officer were killed from the Special Police, and a third RS police officer had his hand burned and was wounded and being treated. And, of course, down the line, when Colonel Borovcanin who was present at that location explained that, so, I mean, I am aware of it, but, I mean, the older question or the broader question with respect to Kravica, whether it was a premeditated act or what, whether it was a reactionary act, as I've testified in the Karadzic case, I believe that what predicated it isn't as important as the outcome. Even if I were to accept a premise that the shooting at Kravica warehouse started as a result of an attempt by Muslims who were detained there to escape, one, I am aware of survivor testimony from witnesses there who talk about the executions occurring in waves over a space of several hours, and I'm also aware of the casualties there, in the sense that when one looks at the number of prisoners who were held at Kravica warehouse and their outcomes; for example, if one takes an easy mathematical number of a thousand being detained at the Kravica warehouse, there are three known survivors. There are multiple possible outcomes for people held in the warehouse in -- when the shooting starts: They are either instantaneously killed; they are wounded and die even with medical intervention; they are wounded but will survive with medical intervention; or they are unwounded or so slightly wounded that they don't require medical intervention. Just as a function of statistical probability, what you have is out of a population of a thousand, you have 997 who are killed, and you have, on the other end of the spectrum, three who survive. You have no members of the population group in the middle who were taken to Bratunac medical centre and died of their wounds or who were taken to Bratunac medical centre and survived their wounds. Consequently, when one looks at the outcome, my view is that the inescapable conclusion was that regardless of how the Kravica warehouse massacre started, at some juncture a decision was made that all of the people who were held at that location were going to be killed. The end result of that can offer no other conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is it your testimony that the decision that all of them would be killed occurred after the attempted break through and the fire-fight?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when that decision was made. Individuals have testified with respect to that. I don't know when that decision was made. All I can do, again, is recount that at some juncture, the decision had to have been made simply based on the results.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Can the results of your investigation exclude the possibility that the decision was made by those policemen physically present at the Kravica site after the attempted escape and after the fire-fight between armed detainees and the guards?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the witness says that he can't say whether it was before or after, that means that he doesn't exclude the possibility that it was after. Mr. Ivetic, to that extent, the question has been answered. Further, the question was composite by including those who would have made the decision, which was not yet part of the previous testimony. So if you want to further pursue that, at the same time if the witness doesn't know when the decision was taken, it's likely but you could further explore that who would have taken such a decision. Do you know whether who took that decision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir. I mean, again I can catalogue who was there by rank and position but I cannot testify as to who made the decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Since you can catalogue who was there by rank and position, would you agree with me that no officer of the VRS was present?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, you're asking me now to speculate on an unknown. I am aware that many of the people there were police. Certainly at least one member of the Red Beret were there and I am aware of information that other members of the Bratunac military police may have been there at some point. I can't -- again, I'm not aware of any VRS officers being there at 1700 when or even shortly thereafter, when the massacre occurred, but again I can't exclude that possibility simply because I just -- I'm sure I don't know all of the facts related to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you know from your investigation, and can you confirm, that prior to this event, prior to this date, there were no organised executions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would disagree. I testified prior that I consider the Jahorina -- sorry, let me try that one again. The Jadar River massacre to be evidence of an organised execution.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Perhaps we misunderstood each other. In relation to Kravica, before this date, before --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you're talking before 13 July?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct, correct.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, the mass executions, there were no -- to my knowledge, there were no mass executions that occurred on 12 July. So 13 July would be the beginning of the series of mass executions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the -- you indicated a person from the Red Berets, I believe from your revised written narrative I remember reading something that he may have been travelling on the road, passing by Kravica, when he was wounded?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, from my narrative, I don't believe I speculate as to how he got there, simply I note the fact that there is a document from the Bratunac medical centre that places him there. As I recall, we -- after we learned about the fact that he was there, we did try to interview him, and his -- if I recall correctly, what we discovered was that several years after the war he perished in an automobile accident.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you be surprised if I told you that this incident in Kravica does not appear in your narrative at all?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which one?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The revised narrative.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The most recent one.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, a lot of the information that we received pertaining to the circumstances came after 2003, in my -- so again, as I've said, some of the issues are in the narrative, some of them would be in other documents, but I have testified about that because I think a lot of that information came to light at the Tribunal after my departure and coming up to the trial of Borovcanin, who was part of the Popovic trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I agree with you as to the dates and my question is, it's not in your narrative, you didn't testify about it during direct examination, how did you think that this Chamber was going to get that very important information to assess what actually is in your narrative if you don't offer it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm confused by your question. The information that is my narrative is the most complete information that I had at the time of publication. As I've testified before, one of the techniques that the Office of the Prosecutor uses is to introduce documents related to these particular issues in my subsequent testimony. Again, I don't control what the Office of the Prosecutor does or does not choose to lead me through my testimony. It's his ten hours, not mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So would you agree with me that to get a full and as accurate as possible picture of your knowledge and conclusions, it would be necessary for myself, as I did, and for the Chamber, to review all of your prior testimonies rather than to rely upon just the written reports and just the direct examination in this case?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I would reply that that is entirely dependent upon the ultimate determination of this Trial Chamber or any past Trial Chamber as to how much to rely or not rely on the information that I provide as part of their ultimate decision process.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But you will agree with me that for the Chamber to know what there is to rely upon they would need to know the entirety of it and that entirety is not in your reports?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, this is getting very vague and the references and speculative, and it's unnecessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We have been talking about a specific incident. We are talking about a specific incident that he's gone through in great detail. It's not vague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, Mr. Ivetic, would you not interrupt Mr. McCloskey, not only for Mr. McCloskey but also for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, was it your intention to primarily draw the attention of the Chamber that a report which is not updated in respect of such new information, that that would be cumbersome for the Chamber to rely upon? Because if that was your intention, then you succeeded.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I also would like then to draw the Chamber's attention to the fact that it also goes towards the -- whether the person is an expert, whether they are -- whether they have a bias. And if they don't bring forward information and the Defence has to pull it out of them I think that goes towards that consideration as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You consider that to be bias and that's what you want to bring to the attention of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. And if that's clear then I can move on to a different topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's clear that you've drawn the attention of the Chamber to it and that you consider it to be bias. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to look at the revised Srebrenica Military Narrative which is 65 ter number 4627 and I'd like to focus on page 6 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, from -- I apologise, page 1 in both languages - there we go - which is page -- page 1 in the text which is page 6 in e-court. Now I know where I'm going. Sir, this section that is entitled, "executive summary" goes from page 6 in e-court for five pages which should get us to page 11 in e-court, and in this section there are no references to either intercepts or documents or witness testimony that would support the assertions. Would you agree with me, sir, that this is a different format and different approach than for the other reports on the brigade, corps and Main Staff levels which you authored for use at trial?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. Again, I believe I have executive summaries in all of those products. Part of my military background, the formats that we use in reports are obviously to include an executive summary. I certainly recall being cross-examined by Mr. Haynes, I believe, for the better part of a session as to why I did not footnote my executive summary. And I think at the end of the day my answer was that, I mean, it's a summary of the information and that what I expect is that any reader of the document would go to the base document or the base paragraphs in the various sections of the narrative and the documents that I do cite in those to rely on for certain issues. An executive summary is just that, it's a quick executive summary. It's not a substantive component of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me from your military intelligence background that these executive summaries or situation reports or sit-reps are meant to apprise a commander of something without their having to read the entire remainder of the report and to urge a particular course of action in essence to advocate for the commander to accept the facts reported therein and act in accordance with a -- to adopt a course of action in accordance with the facts as set forth in the summary?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The one thing I don't do, however, is I do not assume that a general officer or a commander who is pressed for time is the same as triers of fact and law who will, I take it, go through the entire document because they are ultimately responsible for assuming the decision of the guilt or innocence of an accused. They are not going to do that based off of a six-page executive summary of a 100-page document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now I'd like to move to some preliminary methodological observations in reference to your Brigade Command Responsibility Report, and that is 65 ter number 04624. Now that we have it on the screen, if we could turn to page 4.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir, you said the brigade or corps command report is the one I'm looking at on the screen, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm looking for the brigade report. I apologise. It should be number 04625. I misspoke. And now if we can go to page 4 in both versions, and I'd like to focus on the paragraph at the top, 1.0, it's at the top of both the original and the translation, and reads: "The Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, hereinafter referred to as the Army of the Republika Srpska or the VRS, was formed from the remnants of the former Yugoslav National Army (JNA) which remained in Bosnia following the announced withdrawal of all JNA forces in May 1992." Now, sir, would you agree with me that TO or Territorial Defence units, that in fact made up a considerable part of the Army of the Republika Srpska, especially at the brigade level, cannot be referred to as remnants of the former Yugoslav National Army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not equate Territorial Defence units as being part of the Yugoslav National Army in that sense. My view, though, is that one looks at the leadership and a significant components of the VRS, those officers, the command structures, and even in the case of the 1st Krajina Corps being the former JNA 5th Corps, as well as the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps being at least parts of the former JNA 4th Corps, I believe that my conclusion is sound.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your conclusion doesn't have this detail. Your conclusion does not in this paragraph mention the TO. The TO doesn't factor until the third paragraph where it appears out of the blue. Would you agree with me that as written, this portion of your report is at least misleading, if not inaccurate and contradictory, as written?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess if I'm talking about issues in sequence, the fact that I mentioned the TO in the third paragraph versus the first paragraph, I'm not exactly sure what your point is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Reading your report, someone who is relying upon your report --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I take it they will read the entire report in context and not paragraph by paragraph. I mean, these reports are designed to be read in sequence and completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can return for a moment to that first paragraph, and I'd like to read the remainder of that paragraph, or the next part of it, I should say. Again the first paragraph is 1.0: "As organised at that time, it was comprised of five geographically based corps under the command of the Main Staff, a body composed of a nucleus of senior Bosnian Serb officers from the former JNA 2nd Military District headquarters." Is this meant to imply that the Main Staff of the VRS was in fact the heart or nucleus of the JNA 2nd Military District headquarters transplanted --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What it is --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- to a new organisation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: To a new organisation.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What I'm saying is that many of the key officers who ultimately stood up the Main Staff held correspondingly similar positions from the JNA 2nd Military District when they were assigned there prior to the withdrawal of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask a few follow-up questions in that regard. The JNA 2nd Military District headquarters, when you make reference to that body, would you agree with me that that body, when it existed, had over a hundred officers within its composition? Maybe you as an expert might know the precise number, do you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would suggest that the best information I have and that I would have put forward on the 2nd Military District and their transition would be in the Main Staff report which was written seven years after this, and in some of those notes that I have there, it might have those documents that you're asking. I don't recall off of the top of my head how many officers were in the 2nd Military District at the time of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I understand you don't know the specific number. Do you recall if it was over a hundred?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, if I don't know the specific number, I'd be speculating if I knew it were over a hundred or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's not -- you can say, I don't know whether it was 200 or 300, then you don't know the number, but nevertheless you know that it was more than a hundred. I leave it to that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again -- yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the logic behind it is not compelling. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that at the time of its formation, the Main Staff of the Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, later known as the VRS, was comprised of a total of 12 persons by way of comparison, of whom five were generals?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the origin of the Main Staff I would not disagree with you on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that during the entire duration of the 1992 through 1995 period the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska never attained even half of the number of officers that were within the composition of the JNA 2nd Military District when it existed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I've never done a specific analysis comparing the manpower of that, but I wouldn't disagree with the proposition. I mean, I know from my research historically that not only was the VRS Main Staff understaffed with the qualified officers that it needed, but almost all of the entity, the subordinate levels, suffered from a significant shortage of appropriately skilled officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, if the witness has testified that he doesn't know how many officers there were in the 2nd Military District, how could he possibly answer a question whether in the VRS the number ever went -- never went to half of what is for the witness an unknown number? I mean, apart from putting your questions, listening to the answers, might assist as well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall during the time period of 1992 to 1995 what is the highest staffing level of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska attained in terms of officers?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall a specific number. I know that the Office of the Prosecutor has those documents. And, again, my memory could be refreshed on that because I know that we do have several documents which relate to the manning of the VRS Main Staff at certain points in time during the war. So that information is available.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did the VRS Main Staff ever attain a level of a hundred officers, 50 officers? Do you have any way of narrowing down that unknown number, again based upon your expertise?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, it's been a while since I looked at that specific document. I believe that it may be cited in my Main Staff report, but I just can't give you a number with any degree of confidence, whether it's 60, whether it's 75 or whether it's a hundred. I mean, I know that they obviously had enough officers to do the job, as far as they were concerned, but I also know that from their own reporting, that they didn't feel they had as many officers as they wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see I think we are either at or just before the time period for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we are at the time of the break. Could Mr. Butler be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will almost take a break. Mr. Stojanovic, one question in relation to the earlier request you made for -- the announcement that you would seek a certificate. Could you give us the date and the page reference exactly where, as you said, after the delivery of the decision of the Chamber, that you put that motion orally, I take it, at the time to decide on the matter?
